subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Coaching notes, session 4. Written by Maria, leadership coach.
Dilnaz (26) has led the design team at the agency for five months. I asked about the 360-degree feedback that came in last week.
She waved the printout. 'Two people said I don't listen. Honestly? One of them wanted this role. It's jealousy. The other one just doesn't have the vision for where we're going.'
I asked about the comment that her deadlines were unrealistic. 'Clients like ambition,' she said. 'People who can't keep up always call it unrealistic.'
When I asked whether any of the feedback might be useful, she smiled politely and moved on to her plans for a new logo system.
What I notice: every critical remark is explained by the other person's motive, never checked against what happened. Two projects have slipped this quarter.
Next session: I'll ask her to pick one piece of feedback and look only at the facts behind it.

qa.q: How many people said Dilnaz doesn't listen?
qa.a: Two people said Dilnaz doesn't listen.

qa.q: Why might Dilnaz be so quick to call the feedback jealousy?
qa.a: She seems to feel threatened by criticism, because admitting it might crack the confident new-leader identity she is protecting.

qa.q: What is Maria's plan for the next session, and why might it help?
qa.a: Maria will ask Dilnaz to pick one piece of feedback and look only at the facts, which makes it harder to dismiss it by blaming motives.

qa.q: How might the two people who gave feedback feel if they heard Dilnaz call it jealousy?
qa.a: They may feel insulted and decide it isn't worth being honest with her again.

grounding: It shows a new leader brushing off critical feedback as jealousy or lack of vision, protecting her new identity and no longer learning.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
Thursday night.
Aditi stopped me after the review today and said, very carefully, that the new approval process I set up is confusing people. That three vendors have complained. That it takes four days now instead of two.
Honestly. She has been like this since I got the role. She applied for it too, everyone knows that. Of course she thinks my process is bad.
And the vendors? They'll adjust. People always complain about change. The ones who can't see why we need it just aren't thinking big enough.
Riyaz said something similar last week. I told him it was a teething problem. He didn't bring it up again, which proves my point.
I'm not going to change a process just because a few people are unhappy. That's what weak leads do.
Still, four days. I'll check the numbers. Maybe next month.
— Zainab

qa.q: How long does approval take now, according to Aditi?
qa.a: It takes four days now instead of two.

qa.q: Why does Zainab decide Aditi's feedback comes from jealousy?
qa.a: Zainab feels threatened by the criticism and finds it easier to blame Aditi's motives than to admit the new process might be wrong.

qa.q: What went wrong in how Zainab handled the feedback, and what could fix it?
qa.a: Zainab treated every challenge as an attack and stopped learning; checking the four-day figure this week and asking Riyaz and the vendors for details would help.

qa.q: What is it like for Riyaz after his concern was called a teething problem?
qa.a: Riyaz may feel brushed off and decide it's pointless to raise problems with Zainab again.

grounding: It shows a new lead brushing off critical remarks as jealousy or narrow thinking, treating challenge as a threat and so no longer learning.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
At 1 a.m., two hours before the app update was due to go live, the office generator coughed and the lights dimmed. Varun, lead for four months, was pacing between desks when Samir said, "The login change hasn't been tested on slow networks. I think we should hold the release a day."
Varun didn't stop pacing. "You always find a reason to slow things down, Samir."
"I'm saying it because half our users are in small towns."
"And I'm saying it because I can see the bigger picture." Varun looked round the room. "Some people just aren't comfortable with speed."
Samir turned back to his screen. Nobody else spoke.
In the cab home at 4 a.m., after pressing release, Varun replayed the moment. Samir had always been a bit jealous, hadn't he? Ever since the promotion. That was all it was. He felt a knot in his stomach and decided it was tiredness.

qa.q: What had not been tested, according to Samir?
qa.a: The login change, on slow networks.

qa.q: What was Varun feeling when he decided Samir was jealous?
qa.a: He felt threatened and uneasy, with a knot in his stomach, and protected his new image by calling the warning jealousy.

qa.q: What turning point is available to Varun at this stage?
qa.a: He could call Samir the next day, ask exactly what worried him, and test the login on slow networks before users complain.

qa.q: How might Samir feel after being told he always slows things down?
qa.a: Samir probably feels dismissed and embarrassed in front of the team, and less willing to raise concerns next time.

grounding: Under release-night pressure, a new lead brushes off a warning as jealousy and a lack of nerve, protecting his image and learning nothing.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
In the weekly review at their Kolkata office, Rekha said carefully, "Jagdish, the client's research says their buyers are over fifty. The campaign we're pitching is all short videos for teenagers. I'm worried we're missing them."
Jagdish smiled the smile he had started using since becoming lead. "That's exactly the old thinking this client wants to escape, Rekha. Vision means seeing where they should go, not where they are."
Two juniors nodded. Rekha said nothing more.
Later, a senior designer raised the same concern at the coffee machine. Jagdish laughed. "Everyone suddenly has opinions now that I'm lead." He went back to his desk and wrote in his notebook: Team resisting change. Needs stronger direction.
He didn't open the research file again. He had read it once, before the promotion.

qa.q: What does the client's research say about their buyers?
qa.a: Their buyers are over fifty.

qa.q: What does Jagdish's note 'Team resisting change' reveal about his mindset?
qa.a: He feels defensive and threatened by challenges, treating concern as resistance so his new identity as the visionary stays safe.

qa.q: What could Jagdish do instead of writing that note?
qa.a: Reopen the research file and ask Rekha and the designer to walk him through their worry before the pitch.

qa.q: How does Rekha experience being told she has old thinking?
qa.a: Rekha likely feels dismissed and a little humiliated, and learns that careful warnings are not welcome.

grounding: A new lead brushes off critical remarks as old thinking and jealousy, protecting his new identity and no longer learning.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage:
"Can I say something about the rota, Damini?"
"Sure, Avni. Quick, though."
"The new night rota. People are exhausted. Three of the front-desk staff asked me to talk to you because they're scared to."
"Scared? Of me?" Damini laughed. "Come on. I know what's going on. Some people haven't accepted that I'm manager now."
"That's not it. It's the back-to-back nights."
"The rota works on paper. I checked it twice."
"On paper, yes. At the hotel desk at 4 a.m., it's different."
"You know what I think? You wanted this job too. It's fine. I get it."
Avni was quiet for a second. "I didn't want your job. I wanted you to hear this."
"Noted," Damini said, already looking at her phone. "Anything else?"
"No," Avni said. "Nothing else."

qa.q: How many front-desk staff asked Avni to talk to Damini?
qa.a: Three of the front-desk staff.

qa.q: Why does Damini say Avni wanted the job too?
qa.a: Damini feels threatened by the criticism and protects her new identity by explaining it away as jealousy.

qa.q: What could Damini have done when Avni raised the rota?
qa.a: Asked what happens at the desk at 4 a.m. and invited the three staff to talk, instead of calling the concern jealousy.

qa.q: What is it like for Avni when she says 'Nothing else'?
qa.a: Avni feels hurt and shut out, and will probably stop bringing the team's concerns to Damini.

grounding: A newly promoted hotel manager dismisses a colleague's warning about the rota as jealousy, protecting her image and shutting out feedback.

subtopic: A promotion and the ego that follows
passage: I'm Pranav, and three weeks after they made me design lead, Chandrika stopped me outside the pantry. She said the new onboarding flow had too many steps and that two clients had already complained. I remember smiling at her. In my head I was already sorting it: she had wanted this role, she had applied for it too, so of course she would find holes. I told her, "Some people just don't see where we're going yet." She nodded and walked off. That night I told my flatmate the team resented change. When a junior raised the same point in the review, I thought, great, now she's lobbying. Looking back even a little, what bothers me is how certain I felt. Every question sounded like an attack on the title I had only just got used to.

qa.q: Who stopped Pranav outside the pantry?
qa.a: Chandrika stopped Pranav outside the pantry.

qa.q: How did Pranav feel when Chandrika criticised the onboarding flow?
qa.a: Pranav felt defensive and a little superior, reading her point as jealousy because she had applied for the same role.

qa.q: What could Pranav do now to catch this pattern?
qa.a: Pranav could go back to the two client complaints and check the facts separately from who raised them, then ask Chandrika to walk through the steps with them.

qa.q: How might Chandrika see that exchange by the pantry?
qa.a: Chandrika probably felt brushed aside and may decide it is not worth warning Pranav again, even when something serious comes up.

grounding: Shows a new lead brushing off criticism as jealousy, protecting a fresh identity and no longer learning from the team.
